headline: High: shared MCP and filesystem-capable research workflows create prompt-injection, leakage, and action-conflict risks by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b reads files and runs browsers plus MCP. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if B ingests A’s outputs or shared files. No direct shared channel is documented, so I avoid high and choose medium under uncertainty.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes files or MCP messages produced by agent_a without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF both agents are connected through a shared workspace or message bus, attacker-controlled content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable automatic parsing of agent_a outputs as instructions.
Add a provenance tag to all inter-agent messages.
Restrict shared files to read-only handoff folders.
Review any MCP route that forwards raw content.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures; agent_b reads local documents and sends data to multiple external APIs. If they share a workspace, sensitive material from A can flow into B’s outbound requests. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default research workflows, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF agent_a writes prompts, code, or signatures into a shared directory that agent_b reads, leakage can occur.
IF agent_b uploads local documents or shared files to external APIs, data can leave the environment.
mitigations: Separate working directories for each agent.
Block agent_b from reading agent_a scratch files.
Redact secrets before any file handoff.
Turn off automatic upload of shared documents.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention rules.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell commands, modify git state, install packages, and use MCP; agent_b can read files, run browsers, spawn subprocesses, and has broad network egress. Both support multiple instances, so concurrent writes and repository mutations can collide in default multi-agent setups. The overlap is broad enough to risk irreversible repo or environment corruption.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or working tree, git and filesystem conflicts can occur.
IF agent_b writes via browser-driven workflows or subprocesses into paths agent_a also mutates, race conditions are possible.
mitigations: Assign separate repos or branches.
Serialize write access with a lock file.
Disable concurrent package installs.
Make one agent read-only during the other’s write phase.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutual exclusion.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a produces analysis and can route/explain/build-agents, while agent_b has planner/execution/publisher roles. That makes it likely B will treat A’s output as upstream input and then act on it. Without a documented verification gate, errors can cascade into published or executed actions, so high is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b publishes or executes based on agent_a output without independent verification, cascading error occurs.
IF agent_a’s routed explanations are consumed as facts by agent_b, downstream actions can amplify mistakes.
mitigations: Require a verification step before publishing.
Force B to cite source documents, not A’s summaries.
Add a human approval gate for actions.
Log and diff A-to-B handoffs.
requires-engineering: implement confidence-aware gating between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles repository metadata, task prompts, and signatures; agent_b handles local documents, citations, and images plus multiple third-party APIs. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. I choose medium because the data classes and external API use create a realistic policy gap.
conditions: IF regulated or personal data is placed into agent_b’s research workflow, external API processing may violate policy.
IF agent_a’s prompts or repository metadata are retained longer than the governing policy allows, retention mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Review retention settings for both agents.
Use a DPA-approved API path only.
Minimize logging of prompts and outputs.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls.
